titre: The Hadza Burn as Many Calories as We Do, Mass for Mass
accroche: Bow hunting, foraging, miles on foot: for equal lean mass, the Hadza expend as much energy per day as a Westerner.
contenu_vulgarise:
In northern Tanzania, the Hadza live in a wooded savanna. They hunt with bows, dig up tubers, gather berries and baobab fruit, and harvest honey, with no vehicles and no firearms. During the study, more than 95% of their calories came from wild foods. You would expect them to expend far more energy than someone living in an industrialized country, and the idea plays a part in the debate over obesity: the Western way of life supposedly lowers daily energy expenditure, and weight follows.

## Measuring Without Disturbing

In 2012, Herman Pontzer and his colleagues tested this hypothesis with the doubly labeled water method: subjects drink water whose hydrogen and oxygen atoms can be tracked, and how fast those atoms leave the body in urine makes it possible to calculate total energy expenditure, in kilocalories per day, without interfering with their daily routines. The team followed 30 Hadza adults (13 men aged 18 to 65, 17 women aged 18 to 75) for 11 days, and compared their measurements with those of 186 women and 53 men from North America and Europe, and with those of farming populations.

## More Active, but Not Bigger Energy Spenders

The physical activity level, calculated as the ratio of total expenditure to estimated basal metabolic rate, is higher among the Hadza, markedly so for men: 2.26 versus 1.81 for the Western men in the sample (for women, the gap is narrower: 1.78 versus 1.68). Yet once lean mass is taken into account, the Hadza's total daily expenditure does not differ from that of Westerners, for either women or men. The energy cost of walking and of resting, relative to mass, is comparable as well. The farming populations in the sample (Nigeria, Gambia, Bolivia) are the exception: they expend more than the other groups at equal mass.

Part of the explanation lies in body size: the Hadza are smaller, averaging 43 kg for women and 51 kg for men, versus 74 and 81 kg for the Westerners in the sample. Their body fat percentage is also lower, but it does not vary with activity level in this data set.

## A Body That Compensates

A 2015 study of the Hadza, with GPS units worn by 41 adults, finds no link between distance traveled, workload, and total expenditure once lean mass is taken into account. The authors suggest that very active adults may adapt by reducing the energy allocated to other physiological functions. In 2016, across 332 adults from five populations, total expenditure rises with activity at low levels, then plateaus at high levels: a “constrained” model.

None of this means that moving around is pointless. The authors of the 2012 study point out that their work is not an intervention study and that physical activity has positive effects on health. They also consider their results consistent with the idea that differences in obesity between populations come mostly from what people eat rather than from what they expend. In 2015, the team found a higher marker of metabolic stress among the Hadza than in industrial populations, though the measurements do not yet say where the energy is being reallocated.

repere.texte: In 30 Hadza adults followed for 11 days with doubly labeled water, the physical activity level is higher than in Westerners (2.26 versus 1.81 for men), but daily energy expenditure, at equal lean mass, does not differ.
repere.source: Pontzer et al., “Hunter-gatherer energetics and human obesity,” PLoS ONE, 7 (7), e40503, 2012

carte.punch: More active, the Hadza still burn as many calories per day as we do, mass for mass.
carte.idee: Measured for 11 days with doubly labeled water, 30 Hadza adults are more active than Westerners (activity level 2.26 versus 1.81 for men), yet burn as many calories per day at equal lean mass. The body seems to compensate.

quiz.question: What does the measurement of the Hadza's daily energy expenditure, compared with that of Westerners, show?
choix: It is markedly higher among the Hadza, who walk and hunt every day
It is lower among the Hadza, whose resting metabolism is slower
It is similar at equal lean mass, even though the Hadza's activity level is higher
It is similar because the Hadza eat mostly industrial foods, like us
quiz.explication: At equal lean mass, the Hadza's total expenditure does not differ from that of Westerners, even though their activity level is higher: the body seems to compensate. Their resting metabolism per kilo is comparable, and more than 95% of their calories came from wild foods during the study.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What method allows Pontzer and his colleagues to measure the Hadza's total energy expenditure in 2012 without disrupting their days?
choix: Doubly labeled water, whose elimination in urine makes it possible to calculate total expenditure
GPS units worn continuously for eleven days
A calorimeter set up in a temporary camp
A daily questionnaire about the activities performed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The method is doubly labeled water: subjects drink water with trackable atoms, and total expenditure in kilocalories per day is calculated from their elimination in urine, without interfering with their activities. The GPS units were used only in the 2015 study.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the 2012 sample, which group expends more energy than the others at equal mass?
choix: Hadza men, because of bow hunting
The Western women in the comparison sample
The farming populations of Nigeria, Gambia, and Bolivia
Hadza children, who accompany the adults foraging
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The farming populations in the sample, Nigeria, Gambia, and Bolivia, are the exception: they expend more than the other groups, Hadza and Westerners included, at equal mass. Hadza men, for their part, do not expend more than Westerners at equal lean mass.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the authors of the 2015 study, conducted with GPS units worn by 41 Hadza adults, suggest to explain the lack of a link between distance traveled and total expenditure?
choix: That the most active Hadza eat more to compensate for the effort
That very active adults may reduce the energy allocated to other physiological functions
That GPS-measured distances are systematically underestimated among the Hadza
That total expenditure depends only on fat mass, never on activity
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The authors suggest that very active adults may adapt by reducing the energy allocated to other physiological functions, which would explain the lack of a link between distance traveled, workload, and total expenditure once lean mass is taken into account.
